prize_parts.citation: For developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how lobbying and special-interest politics shape trade protection.

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred part from B002 to B001. The change rests on three points from the exchange and my own round-1 reasoning, not on the number of members who prefer B001. First, my main objection to B001 in round 1 was citation scope. I did not want the growth-and-trade strand folded in by implication, since it goes beyond the ballot's stated discovery and may overlap with recent recognition (an overlap that the files assert and I have not verified). Andersson, Enflo, Fredriksson and Hassler all anchor the citation narrowly on lobbying and trade protection, and I would support only that version. With the scope settled, the contribution is a single discovery: trade protection as the equilibrium outcome of organised political pressure, in a tractable general-equilibrium model with testable implications. Second, attribution. A two-name award from a long joint programme needs no arbitrary exclusions. By my own test of durable change, clarity of credit and maturity, that is a real advantage over B002, where five colleagues independently raised the Bresnahan and Reiss omission and the separation of Pakes's dynamic-games work, and nobody argued that the BLP credit is as clean. Third, as a macroeconomist who builds computational tools, I see in B002 a pull toward methods I know. Part of the reason I ranked it first was that bias. The framework contribution in B001 and the method contribution in B002 differ in kind. On the criteria I apply to every field, B001 now comes out ahead because its credit is cleaner, not because its empirical record is stronger.
statement.case_against: My round-1 concern about the empirical record of protection-for-sale has not gone away. Estimated structural parameters are specification-sensitive and support for the functional forms is mixed, so part of the case is that this is an organising theory that made lobbying measurable, not a confirmed quantitative result. B002's contribution has been validated by thirty years of operational use in merger review and antitrust, and I still think that counts for it on durability of influence. Whether an organising framework with mixed testing is prize-sized is a judgement, and I could be wrong about it either way. Helpman's separate credit on B030 leaves open whether the committee prefers to honour trade through the firm-heterogeneity line. B001 also has to be distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize and from the 2025 growth prize. Both claims are reported in the files and not independently verified by me. B002 is the stronger candidate if the committee decides that a framework whose headline predictions only partly survive testing is not a sufficient discovery.

responses.point: Fredriksson separates the model's value as a framework from the empirical success of its particular predictions, arguing that making lobbying a precise, testable object is what allowed later work to qualify and sometimes contradict it. He would confine the citation to lobbying and trade protection.
responses.response: In round 1 I said I found the mixed record more worrying than he does. I now accept part of his answer. A framework that generates sharp restrictions, and a large body of work that tests and sometimes rejects them, has done what a theory contribution should do. I still do not read the mixed record as confirmation, and I would not want the citation to imply it. His narrow wording, which says nothing about empirical validation, is the one I support, and it is why I can move to B001. His observation that BLP identification rests on strong assumptions, which he raised against B002, is also fair. I take it as a limit on my own first choice and not as an argument against his.

responses.point: Hassler anchors the B001 citation on the stated discovery, the political economy of trade protection, and declines to make the endogenous-growth strand the basis of the award because of overlap with the 2025 recognition. He also asks for a closer look at how much of B002's value lies in Pakes's dynamic-games work versus the BLP demand framework.
responses.response: I agree with the drafting choice. It is the condition under which I support B001, since broadening the citation would blur the credit in the way I objected to in round 1. On his question about B002, the BLP demand framework is the part with the clearest credit and the broadest reach beyond industrial organisation. Pakes's dynamic-games work is a related but partly separate strand, and under a three-name cap the exclusion of Bresnahan and Reiss is a real cost to the citation. I cannot resolve that within the cap, and I take it as a reason B002 is a less stable award than B001, not as a defect in the science.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B002 second and says that if the committee wants an applied-methods prize he would support a BLP triple as the next best configuration. He also notes that Bresnahan and Reiss laid the empirical-IO foundations and that structural versus design-based identification debates remain open.
responses.response: We reached the same reading of B002 from different sides. He is closer to the field and I am closer to the method, and we both find its practical reach large but its credit boundaries less clean than B001's. I am glad to keep it as my first alternative with a BLP triple, and his stated fallback suggests that is a stable configuration if B001 stalls. I do not claim that B002 is weaker on merit. The difference between B001 and B002 is attribution, and that is the question on which I changed my mind.

responses.point: Dreber prefers B030 over B001 because the firm-heterogeneity framework has been confronted with micro data more densely, and she treats mixed support for protection-for-sale as a reason to prefer it. She names the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum omission as its main weakness.
responses.response: Her argument bears on the empirical standing that worries me about B001, and I give it weight. For me it falls short for two reasons. The attribution gap she names would still have to be closed within a three-name citation, and I do not see how to close it without weakening the Melitz-Helpman core. And I do not think denser testing makes B030 a replacement for B001. The two credit different achievements by the same person. If the committee chose to recognise trade through B030, I would want the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum question settled before any vote.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson accepted my attribution point and now proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson, worded around technology and trade shocks to labour demand and not around a task-theory discovery. She reads the revisions of China-shock estimates as evidence of maturity.
responses.response: Her revised citation answers the attribution objection I made, and the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio is a more stable set than the one she opened with. I see the decade of independent re-estimation as a sign of durability, and I withdraw any suggestion in round 1 that revision counts against the work. My remaining difference is about timing and design. The size and persistence of the long-run effects are still being revised, and shift-share identification is still contested. I would also say, as I did for B002, that a design-based contribution and a framework contribution are different in kind and the committee should say which it is rewarding. I do not rank B018 above B001 this year, but I would take it seriously in a later one.

uncertainties: How much weight a prize citation can bear for a framework whose headline predictions are only partly supported in testing, and whether the committee will see that as a limit on the discovery or a normal feature of a productive agenda.
Whether B001 is sufficiently distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize and from the 2025 growth prize. I rely on the files for descriptions of both and have not independently verified them.
Whether the committee will treat Helpman's credit on B001 and B030 as separate achievements or as competing framings of one trade prize, and whether a split would hurt B001.
Whether the BLP triple (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) is the right core for B002, or whether Bresnahan should displace Levinsohn. I leave that unresolved as a reason it is a named alternative.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and colleagues' stated facts. I have not independently verified citation or impact data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Helpman or Grossman, the credited names on my preferred B001. My listed co-authors (Hassler, Boppart, A. Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski, Olovsson) are not credited on B001. For transparency, Hassler (committee chair) and Boppart are close collaborators and IIES colleagues, and Hassler supports B001. I do not treat that as a candidate-specific tie. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Kiyotaki or Moore. My Söderberg professorship and climate-economy work are not tied to any credited name here. I disclose these and do not adjudicate them.
